title: I can't code, should I start with a no-code engine or an AI prototype tool?
author: HourLow5264
selftext:
I've got a folder of game ideas and exactly zero coding ability. not rusty, not "i did html once." just zero!
tried GDevelop twice this month becuase people keep saying it's beginner friendly. the event sheet thing felt like learning a whole new language when all i wanted was to test one mechanic. same deal with Construct. spent a free night clicking around the editor instead of finding out if the idea was fun.
And these are tiny ideas. a 2d jump thing, a card rule test, a puzzle loop. nothing to ship.
I tried a rough Combos prototype for one of the tiny ideas, and it helped me feel the mechanic faster. but i still dk if that'sactually smart or if it just delays learning a real tool. not trying to skip the hard part, just wanted to test before committing.
Basicly want to know if one mechanic is worth touching again, before i sink three weeks into learning a tool that might be wrong for me. Where's the split happen? do you learn a no-code engine from day one, or use an AI prototype tool first to get a rough playable and rebuild later if the idea survives?
I have maybe 5 hours a week. spending them learning menus before testing the idea is starting to feel backwards.

comments.author: zenmatrix83
comments.body:
if you actually want to learn coding try this

[https://scratch.mit.edu/ideas](https://scratch.mit.edu/ideas)

but nothing wrong with trying ai, but start small make pong. Just two paddles with a ball , finsih it., attempt to understand the code at least a little. Then work on making something harder.

You'll get more progress knowing what to ask ai for vs pure vibe coding

I game development its easy to want to get to the game, but you need to build up systems and stuff to work with each other. Don't focus on creating skyrim or even mario brothers. Start with a simple concept till you can reliable create those then "level up" to more complicated things

comments.author: mallcopsarebastards
comments.body: the truth is you're going to have to learn the fundamentals. An agentic coding tool will write the code for you, but if you don't understand how it works you'll get to the half-way mark and find that the tools will have built a brittle architecture and you'll end up with a very buggy game.

replies.author: Accomplished-Read965
replies.body:
True for now - I really wonder how long this will be that case. Interestingly, the model knows everything about architecture much better than me. But when programming it somehow misses to implement it in the same way it actually knows.

If it created something stupid and you ask it what it thinks of it it mostly identifies it correctly as bad and suggests better alternatives. While it programmed it like that in the first place.

So it knows how to do better, but it just doesn't. That's a really interesting behavior...

replies.author: mallcopsarebastards
replies.body:
we will never get to a point where transformer based models no longer need human guidance in the same way human devs still depend on peer code review. These are deterministic systems that can  make mistakes. In order to detect mistakes, you have to know how to identify them. You wouldn't ask a carpenter to review source code, because you need to understand software. 

it's entirely possible that we will end up with models that don't need guidance, but that would have to be an entirely different model architecture because hallucination is an inherent property of the transformer architecture.

comments.author: daddywookie
comments.body:
Welcome to the clash of AI and game development. There are no easy answers and success is earned through effort and study. AI can help with many things but it can’t create it all for you.

Firstly, you are going to have to get a grasp on some programming fundamentals. Even if you don’t touch the code directly you’ll have to know about loops, objects, arrays and variables, front end vs back end and various other things. Without these it is hard to properly interrogate what your AI is planning. The no code tools like GDevelop can help here, or spend some time with a beginners programming course.

Next up, you have to learn to drive your AI tools properly. Define your requirements, break them down into useful chunks, decide what order to work in, how you will get them built, how you will test them, how you will feedback into your agents. If you are familiar with software development this offers a good framework.

Finally, you’ll have to know some game design basics, both for the experience you want to build and also how certain mechanics work. There’s many books available as PDFs online that will give you some basics.

So, if you just want to build isolated mechanics you can just throw credits at it and you’ll get something. If you want to build a game which is a fun experience you’ll have to do a lot more work. It will all pay off though, even failure is a useful learning point.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
